paragraphs.text: ORIGEN: SELECTIONS ON THE PSALMS (50).
PSALM 9.
Verse 8. He has prepared his throne for judgment.
Verse 9. And he himself will judge the world in righteousness; he will judge the peoples with uprightness.

Such a judge, then, is to be feared, and we must flee blameworthy deeds and ungodly thinking. By "the world" (literally, "the inhabited earth") you will understand the Church, which is inhabited by both the Father and the Son, as it is written: "I and my Father will come, and we will make our dwelling with him." By "the peoples" you will understand those who remain outside the Church.
Verse 12. Sing praises to the Lord, who dwells in Zion.

Another interpretation: God dwells in every soul that is a Zion, that is, a watchtower. He seeks out the blood of the nations who shed it, and when he rises up he remembers them. So the words "Their memory has perished with a crash" will refer to the swords. But he remembers those for whom he has become a refuge.
Verse 33. Arise, O Lord my God; let your hand be lifted up; do not forget your poor forever.
Pained by these ungodly words, the prophet prays again, saying this and asking God to show in practice that he has not forgotten the poor. He also reminds him of the blasphemy of the ungodly, saying:
Verse 38. You have heard the desire of the poor, O Lord; turn your ear to the readiness of their heart.

For they desired that the arm of the sinner be broken and that they be set free from his tyranny, and this is what happened. The desire of a good mind is an effective prayer, and when the one who knows hearts saw it, he fulfilled it. For their heart was ready to be saved and to obtain the promised kingdom.
PSALM 13.
Verse 2. The Lord looked down from heaven upon the sons of men, to see whether there is anyone who understands or who seeks God.

Whatever is said of God in bodily terms, since he is in fact bodiless, must be understood in a way worthy of God. For example, he is said to dwell in the heavens because he uses the divine powers in heaven as his temple. For these are called by the same name as the places in which they are, just as human beings are called "earth," as in "Let all the earth worship you" and "All the earth cries out with gladness." He dwells in the heavens also when he is among human beings who bear the image of the heavenly one. And since by his creating and his providence he is present in the whole creation, this is shown through its noblest parts, as in "Our Father who art in heaven," and "God in heaven above." Moreover, in many places of the divine teaching the name "heaven" signifies the intelligible substance, in which above all it is fitting to seek God. For "the heaven of heaven belongs to the Lord." From there, by condescension, he looks upon those in the lower condition, "to see whether there is anyone who understands, who seeks God," so that whoever is found may receive his gifts. This happens when wickedness prevails together with ungodliness, so that it is said: "There is no mercy, no truth, no knowledge of God in the land," and what follows. When people had been harmed in this way, how could the good Savior not look down, so that, finding some beginning of understanding, he might increase it and reveal himself to those who seek him? For he reveals himself to those who do not disbelieve him.
Verse 3. All have turned aside; together they have become worthless.
There is no one who does good, not even one.

He prophesies the change of the nations to gentleness and godliness. That is why he asks: when the Lord has come, will they not cease from their savage way of life and come to know the Lord? For Isaiah also says: "Those who were not told about him will see, and those who have not heard will understand."
Verses 5–6. There they were afraid with fear where there was no fear, for the Lord is in the generation of the righteous.
For there will come a time, he says, when those spoken of before will fear the Lord, among whom there was formerly no fear.
"There" means in the generation to come; it will be established in that generation, of which he speaks [?].
PSALM 15.
Verse 1. A pillar inscription, of David.

The other translators gave the title "Of David," and likewise rendered it "pillar inscription," because the psalm contains a prophecy worthy of everlasting remembrance. For just as the greatest athletes who compete in the stadium are honored with a pillar, and trophies are set up for later remembrance of victories won in war, so the great trophy of the Savior, which he raised when he overthrew the one who held the power of death, was inscribed long beforehand, as on a pillar, in the prophetic Scriptures. That is why Peter too, after quoting what is in this psalm, went on: "Brothers, I may say to you with confidence about the patriarch David that he both died and was buried, and his tomb is with us to this day. Being therefore a prophet, and knowing that God had sworn to him with an oath that from the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh, he would raise up the Christ to sit on his throne, he foresaw and spoke of the resurrection of Christ, that he was not abandoned to Hades, nor did his flesh see corruption. This Jesus God raised up, and of that we are all witnesses."
PSALM 16.
Verse 4. Because of the words of your lips, I have kept to hard ways.

Here too the Savior gives us an example, so that we may not be proud of ourselves, since we need help from God. The paths of the Lord are the keeping of the commandments, or rather the practice of virtue; they become smooth and level from being trodden continually by those who are hurrying to reach their goal, which is blessedness and the fulfillment of the promises. Let us run along them, then, and our steps will not stumble, if the Lord makes them sure in his paths. One who obtained this request says: "Without lawlessness I ran and kept a straight course," and: "I ran the way of your commandments when you enlarged my heart."
PSALM 17.
Verse 6. The pangs of Hades surrounded me; the snares of death overtook me.
These words will also fit the Savior, since they are closely akin to "Now my soul is troubled" and "My soul is very sorrowful, even to death."
Verse 8. And the earth was shaken and trembled, and the foundations of the mountains were troubled and shaken, because God was angry with them.

He plainly shows God's descent on account of what was said before, namely death and the pangs of Hades. When he came down, according to Aquila, the earth was moved and shaken, for every Greek and barbarian ear was filled with his fame. By "the earth" he means those who are on the earth. By "the mountains" he means the hostile powers, which fed upon people with the error of idols and exalted themselves against the knowledge of God. Their foundations, that is, their deep reasonings, sensed the power of the Lord and were troubled and distressed. Because God was angry with these powers, smoke went up as from a firebrand: they were being quenched, and the fire with which they used to burn people was ceasing. He quenched this fire with his own fire, for which reason God is called a consuming fire in Moses. And in the Psalms: "Fire will go before him and burn up his enemies round about." And again: "God will come openly, our God, and will not keep silent; fire will blaze before him, and round about him a mighty tempest." That is why the Savior said: "I came to cast fire on the earth, and how I wish it were already kindled!" He did these things by bowing and coming down, not through one heaven only but through all of them, however many there are. "Bowing" signifies the lowering of his height and the self-emptying of his divinity. The hidden and secret character of his plan of salvation he signifies by the darkness and the mist. Then he was taken up upon the cherub, although he had not come down with it. When the divine powers saw him ascending with his body, they gathered round him and escorted him in his ascent, saying: "Lift up your gates, O rulers, and be lifted up, O everlasting gates, and the King of glory will come in." This happened when, as it is recorded in the Acts of the Apostles, while they were watching he was lifted up, and a cloud took him out of their sight.
Verse 12. And he made darkness his hiding place; round about him was his tent.

Who (52) can see one who is in a tent without going inside? So no one can see God either, unless he enters within the veil of what is hard to comprehend. For Moses too entered the thick darkness where God was. By attending to God's work of creation and his providence, he came to know that God is contained within these. Having opened it a little, he learned from that which is according to the image the one whose image it is, and from creation and providence he learned the Creator and the provider.
PSALM 22.
Verse 3. For his name's sake.
Verse 4. For even if I walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for you are with me.

(53) From this point he turns his words toward God. The one who sits in the shadow of death is settled in it, confirmed in wickedness, and in need of the light that dawns through mercy. But the one who walks passes through it, and the Lord travels along with him. Of sitting it is said: "To those who sat in the region and shadow of death, a light has dawned."
Verse 4. Your rod and your staff, they have comforted me.

Both refer to chastisements, as in the verse: "If your sons forsake my law and do not walk in my judgments, if they do not keep my ordinances, I will punish their transgressions with the rod and their sins with the scourge; but I will not scatter my mercy from them." For God's mercy is not scattered away from the one who is scourged for sin. For (54) the sinner whom he does not scourge, he does not receive; he scourges the son whom he receives. Of those whom he does not scourge it is said: "But as for me, my feet almost slipped; my steps had nearly gone astray. For there is no refusal in their death, and firmness in their scourging. Therefore pride took hold of them; they clothed themselves with their injustice and ungodliness." So if someone is a sinful sheep, he is struck with the rod; if he is a man, with the staff, as Solomon says: "He who spares the staff hates his own son." These comfort the one who is beaten, for he is convinced that he scourges every son whom he receives.
PSALM 23.
Verse 2. And he prepared it upon the rivers.

(55) Another interpretation: before Christ's coming, God was known only in Judea; after it, "the earth is the Lord's." Nor before it was there any "fullness" in all the earth; most of it was full of wickedness. But after it, many of the Gentiles who believed could say: "From his fullness we have all received." For this reason they could also be called his fullness—but not those who are empty of the gospel way of life. Moreover, the sinner dwells in a desert, while the one who dwells in the inhabited world is he who dwells in the Church, which is filled with the Holy Trinity; and he belongs to the Lord. But not so the one who has been born of the devil and has become his portion.
Verse 3. Who shall ascend into the mountain of the Lord, or who shall stand in his holy place?
(56) Or else the mountain of the Lord is the final good, God the Word. For rare is the one who can ascend to its summit through progress.

(57) For the one who has been made perfect, being unable to go any further, stands firm and is called a holy place of God. For walking after the Lord, he ascends, forgetting what lies behind and straining forward to what lies ahead, and his goal is to stand with God in his holy place. Onto this mountain the one who brings good news to Zion must ascend and stand; and when Moses had reached it, God said to him: "But you, stand here with me." And again: "He set my feet upon a rock," as the prophets say, as upon another sanctuary; for the rock was Christ. But who it is that will obtain these promises has been explained more fully in the fourteenth psalm.
Verse 6. This is the generation of those who seek the Lord, who seek the face of the God of Jacob.

(58) And yet he said: "No one shall see my face and live." For truly no one will see it while he is still a man, unless he has put off everything human and been changed into an angel and a god, which does not happen here. But concerning the angels of the little ones in the Church, the Savior says that they "always see the face of the Father who is in heaven."
Verse 9. Lift up your gates, O rulers, and be lifted up, O everlasting gates, and the King of glory will come in.
Verse 10. Who is this King of glory? The Lord of powers, he is the King of glory.

(59) They called him "Lord of powers" as commander of armies; in Hebrew this is said as "Sabaoth." In the Scriptures the Seventy render this both as "Lord of soldiers" and as "Almighty." So what is said here also shows that the Savior is almighty: "Thus says the Lord Almighty: after glory he has sent me to you." For the Father, being almighty, sent the Son who is almighty. And John too says in the Revelation: "Thus says the faithful and true witness, who was and who is and who is to come"—words that admittedly refer to the Savior.
(60) Some, however, say that the words spoken twice refer not to higher gates but to the same gates.
PSALM 27.
Verse 1. To you, O Lord, I will cry; my God, do not keep silent toward me.

If someone asks God for earthly things, he uses a faint voice; but if he asks for heavenly things, he cries out and shouts. That is why in the Scriptures the saints cried out to God. And one cries out when he has gone into his inner room and shut the door. God does not keep silent toward the saints. He spoke, for instance, to Moses, to Aaron, and to Joshua the son of Nun. He spoke also through the prophets, when Israel was his people. What God speaks does not come from outside; it is the holy thoughts that rise up in our heart, as in the verse: "Blessed is the man whose help is from you, O Lord; he has set ascents in his heart." According to Solomon, we have another kind of hearing, a divine perception, which hears the word of God and is united to him. But the one toward whom God keeps silent becomes like those who go down into the pit. For we know of none of the saints who dug a pit; rather, the one who needed water dug a well. Solomon too commands us to drink from wells. But through the prophet God threatens those who drink from pits, saying: "They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water, and dug for themselves broken pits." Those who go down into the pit are those who busy themselves with the cold things of matter; there too dwells the dragon, the enemy of mankind, who is also called cold. For of all the animals on the earth the dragon is the coldest. Every sin, then, is cold, while divine things, it seems, are hot: "He makes his angels spirits and his ministers a flame of fire"; and "I came to cast fire on the earth"; and "fervent in spirit." That sinners are found by pits is shown in Exodus: "God slew, from the face of Pharaoh who sits on the throne to the firstborn of the captive woman who was in the pit." So those who go down into the pit are sinners and captives. But the good God calls even these and grants them release: "For the Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to bring good news to the poor. He has sent me to proclaim release to the captives and recovery of sight to the blind."
Verse 2. Hear, O Lord, the voice of my supplication, when I make supplication to you.

(61) Supplication belongs to those who still lack something. But when, having understood the dignity of God, I ask something of God, then I pray. And when I have become more fully his friend, then I give thanks to God. For Paul too, advancing from the lesser to the greater, says: "I urge, first of all, that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made."
Verse 2. When I lift up my hands toward your holy temple.

Hands lifted up to godly deeds store up treasure in heaven. By them one conquers the spiritual Amalek, just as when Moses raised his hands the people prevailed, but when he let them down, Amalek prevailed. Let us not let our hands down, then, or we shall be defeated.
Verse 5. Because they did not understand the works of the Lord and the works of his hands.
For no one who has not understood the works of the Lord is blameless. For the firmament proclaims the work of his hands, since it enables one to contemplate its Creator by analogy.
Verse 7. And my flesh has flourished again. But what flesh flourished again? "All flesh shall see the salvation of God."
PSALM 36.
Verse 1. Do not provoke the wicked to jealousy, and do not envy those who do lawlessness.

Being jealous and provoking to jealousy are different. To "provoke to jealousy" means to irritate someone and move him to jealousy, as in the verse: "They provoked me to jealousy with what is no god"; that is, they aroused jealousy in me and, as it were, provoked me to anger by their idolatry. To be jealous, or to envy, means to want for oneself what one has judged to be a good belonging to one's neighbor. So this is what he says: do not provoke a wicked man to rise up against you. In other words, do not act in such a way that he conceives a wicked jealousy against you, since then he will plot against you. For example, if the young women had sung the hymn "David has struck down his tens of thousands" with David's consent, then he would have been the one who provoked the wicked man, Saul, to jealousy. Nor, again, should you imitate such people or call them blessed when you see them prospering. For they flourish for a little while and then wither: "All flesh is grass." What, then, do they have that is worth envying, these who flourish for a little while and tomorrow are thrown into the oven, as the Savior says? For I would not say that the passing prosperity of the wicked is in any way worth envying for those who want to live worthily. Rather, one should consider what kind of end will come of choosing to live wickedly. Do not envy such people, then, he says, and do not be stirred up to imitate those who love sin, even if they seem to enjoy the luxuries of this present life. So shun all wavering, looking to what is to come; for things will not always remain as they are. That is why he adds: "For like grass they will quickly wither, and like green herbs they will quickly fall away."
Verse 3. Hope in the Lord and do good, and dwell in the land, and you will be fed with its riches.

(62) That is: love to be approved; thirst to possess the sacred gifts; love the things kept for the saints and stored up with God. "And do good": as if someone said to a field, "Produce this fruit." So to you, the hearer of the divine teachings, the Word says, as to a field [?]: "Do good," which is one of the fruits of the Spirit. Here the word "goodness" denotes every kind of virtue. "And dwell in the land": that is, persevering in the care and cultivation of the soul, "for whatever a man sows, that he will also reap." Perhaps by "the land" he means the divinely inspired Scripture, in which is the wealth of the saints, that is, the promises. And he urges us to hold fast to the divine oracles at all times, out of love for the good things laid up in them for the saints. Or else he has put "dwell" in place of "you will dwell," and by "the land" he clearly means the land promised to the meek; when you are in it, he says, you will be fed upon its riches. The wealth of the city above is the abundant supply of divine gifts. Or perhaps he likens this passing life to a tent, and wants us to use it as a tent on a journey, being its masters and not mastered by it, and using it for what is profitable, not for pleasures. For in this way we shall be fed under the Good Shepherd, enjoying whatever wealth there is in the divine teachings, so that we can say: "The Lord shepherds me, and I shall lack nothing."
Verse 4. Delight yourself in the Lord, and may he give you the requests of your heart.

(63) It is the custom of Scripture to speak of two human beings, and the better one has nearly everything that the worse one has. For there is a food of the inner man too, of which it is said: "Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God." There is also a drink: "For we drink from the spiritual rock that follows us." And there is clothing: so the sinner clothed himself with cursing as with a garment, while the righteous man puts on the Lord Jesus, and a heart of compassion, and the whole armor of God. So the one who only hears his exhortations is nourished; but the one who gives himself to the interpretation of the law, the exposition of the prophets, the solving of the gospel parables, and the clarifying of the apostolic words delights himself in the Lord, and eats not out of necessity, nor merely for nourishment. He teaches us, then, to delight ourselves in the Lord. For God, wishing from the beginning that we should delight in spiritual things, planted the paradise of delight and bestowed the torrent of delight. But no one can delight both in the flesh and in the spirit. If he has delighted in the flesh, like the rich man, he will be deprived of delight with Abraham; but if he has eaten the bread of affliction, like the poor man, there he delights and is at rest.

Another interpretation: the Lord is righteousness, truth, wisdom, sanctification. So if you delight in the contemplations of wisdom and in the deeds of righteousness, the words "Delight yourself in the Lord" are fulfilled. Delight, therefore, is to have dwelling within us God the Word, who gives life to all things, the bread of life; and having him within ourselves, we shall receive all our requests—not just any requests, but those of the heart. You will understand what is said if you personify each of the members of the body and see how each makes requests according to its nature. The eye, if it had a voice, would say to you: "I ask for light; I ask to see colors suited to me." Hearing: "I ask for a melodious, pleasant sound." Taste: "I ask for sweet things; I shun bitter ones." Touch: "I ask to touch what is smooth, soft, and gentle—not fire, not rough things, not things that prick." So, just as each of the senses has its own proper request and its own aversion—the eye asks for light, smell for fragrance, hearing for melody, and the rest likewise—so the heart asks for thoughts, which we shall receive from the Lord if we have nothing in our hearts foreign to delight in him. Then we shall be able to reveal our way to him. For the God of all watches over the pure way of life of those who worship him, but turns away from that of those who do not want to live rightly. Hence he adds:
Verse 5. Reveal your way to the Lord, and hope in him, and he will act.
Verse 6. And he will bring forth your righteousness like light, and your judgment like noonday.

(64) Be one, he says, who openly walks the way that pleases him, that is, who shows God your conduct bare and uncovered; and hope in him, and he will act. In the age to come he will set it forth plainly and make it visible, as it were, on every side, not letting the beauty of your good life go unnoticed. For your righteousness will be evident to all, shining out like the light of noon.

(65) Noonday is the name for the very middle of the day. And he will judge you worthy of light there. Everyone who does evil, the fornicator for example, hates the light, and as far as he can he hides what he does so that it may not be exposed. He wants his fornication to stay unknown, and that is why he also conceals the way he has walked. But the one who does the truth, the chaste man for example, wants to make it manifest. He wants to show it to God, not to men, so that he may not have his reward from men. That is why it is said: Reveal your way to the Lord. That is, show him your blameworthy life, and he will heal you of your wounds and make the filthy clean. And if you become fine and good, he will boast of you. And since you were not vainglorious and hid your righteousness, he himself will make it manifest, and so you will appear (66) like the sun at noon. For then, it says, the righteous will shine like the sun.
Verse 7. Submit to the Lord, and entreat him.

By submission here he means withdrawal from evil things. For no one who sins is submitted to the Lord. Suppose, someone says, that I have already submitted: what am I to do about my former sins? Entreat him, saying: Do not remember our ancient iniquities. So one must not entreat about sin before submitting to the Lord, that is, before departing from sin. For to ask forgiveness of sins while still remaining in sins is utterly unreasonable.
Verse 7. Do not envy the one who prospers in his way, the man who does lawlessness.

Do not imitate, he says, a prosperity built up out of lawlessness. Do not be provoked to wickedness even if you see evil prospering. You should reckon instead that this age belongs to those who have no other hope. Let them be fortunate in it and have the things reckoned good. But we look to another age, an age of life, and our hope lies beyond this age. It is not possible to have good things both in this age and in that one. If anyone has them in this one, he will hear there, while being punished: You received your good things in your lifetime. The words 'the man who does lawlessness' have been added for a necessary reason. It is the imitation of such people, he says, that must be refused, and it is very profitable to keep well away from envying them. For they prosper (67), or rather, they are supposed to enjoy prosperity in their own affairs, though they gain their wealth not by decrees from above but sometimes by greed and by seizing what belongs to others. So by 'prospering' he means advancing toward the worse. Many who live in righteousness see themselves in toil and the sinner prospering in everything for a time, and they grow angry and abandon righteousness, which is the height of folly. For this reason the word teaches patience and tells us to await the fruit of God's righteousness.
Verse 8. Cease from anger, and forsake wrath.

The example is beneficial and most fitting for those submitted to God. For one must, he says, be gentle and thoroughly settled, keeping good order in one's mind, always loving the prosperity that comes from patience and keeping away from the waves of anger. Some of the passions do not befall many people, and even those who happen to have them cast them off as they make progress. But this foul passion, anger, inflames and agitates even those who seem to be wise. It does not trouble some and spare others. I venture to say it troubles all men except the perfect, if anyone perfect is to be found anywhere.
Verse 9. But those who wait for the Lord will inherit the earth.

(68) We are somehow always accustomed to rise up away from wicked deeds when the fear of punishment pushes us toward the better, and to be driven toward living lawfully by desire for the gifts that come from God. For this reason the psalmist, having shown the destructive end of evildoers, adds: Those who wait for the Lord, that is, those who achieve an approved life through endurance and patience, will inherit the earth. This is not a portion of this earth, which has come under a curse and which the one who works it eats in sorrow all the days of his life. It is that other earth, the one prepared for the saints. For their portion is the beautiful city of the saints, holy and on high, whose giver is God. (69) And just as the Savior is wisdom, Word, peace and righteousness, so he is also patience. For it is written: And now what is my patience? Is it not the Lord? From him one may draw and receive everything that, according to the Scriptures, Christ is said to be. As we become righteous and wise and are at peace by participating in him, so too we endure by participating in him. Be still, then, waiting patiently and expecting God, and do not be troubled by present things.
Verse 11. But the meek will inherit the earth.

The followers of Valentinus and certain others think that the Savior says things not said in the old Scriptures. Let them be refuted by this passage when they hear: Blessed are the meek, for they will inherit the earth. It had already been said earlier, through David, by the same Spirit.

(70) With great skill David sets the rewards of the saints alongside the punishments of the lawless. Through these he sharpens them toward a desire for spiritual manliness, through which one may achieve every form of virtue. (71) That is why he says: But the meek will inherit the earth, meaning, clearly, the earth above. For if, according to Paul, there is in the heavens a Jerusalem and a Mount Zion [?], it follows that we should also understand an earth, which those who have conquered a destructive passion [?]. That passion is anger, which destroys even the wise, since they are hindered from acting according to virtue. Gentleness and anger are diametrically opposed to each other. Where there is anger, there is no gentleness at all, and where there is gentleness, there is no anger at all.
Verse 12. The sinner will watch the righteous man and gnash his teeth at him.
Verse 13. But the Lord will laugh him to scorn, for he foresees that his day will come.

From this we learn that the sinner is opposed to the righteous man, just as darkness and light are opposites by nature. So if you see the righteous man hated, do not hesitate to say of the one who hates him that he is a sinner. Those who set their minds on worldly things and have bound their minds to the turmoil of the present life always somehow rage against those who live a pure and choice life, and they consider the lover of righteousness an enemy.
Verse 14. The sinners have drawn the sword, they have bent their bow, to cast down the poor and needy, to slaughter the upright in heart.

Just as there is a full armor of God, so there is a full armor of the devil, which his soldier has put on: the breastplate of unrighteousness, the helmet of destruction, the shield of unbelief, and the sword of the evil spirit. The sinner draws this sword, and his feet run to unrighteousness. There is a readiness of the gospel, and there is also a shoe most ready for sin. Here, then, they have drawn the sword because they have sin close at hand and are ready to commit it. These are the ones who hide the sword of the evil spirit in the scabbard of sin. The arrow of the righteous is Christ Jesus: You have set me as a chosen arrow. The word of sinners is an arrow too. It carries the poison of sin and wounds anyone not armed with the shield of faith. Sinners know that they cannot cast down a rich man who is rich in wisdom and in good works, and so they do not even attack him in the first place. Their whole plot is against the poor man, since a man's own wealth is the ransom of his soul, but the poor man cannot withstand a threat. It is good, then, not to have the sword of sin at all. The second best is, if one has it, not to draw it but to keep it quiet. For when it lies idle it does not merely rust or grow blunt but vanishes entirely. And then we have no need of the fire by which each one's work is tested. That fire does not touch Peter, who instead hears: Even if you pass through fire, the flame will not burn you. But the lake of fire does touch sinners, just as the Red Sea touched the Egyptians but not the Hebrews. The Savior is a chosen arrow, and the saints, corresponding to the Savior, are arrows of God who wound with a chosen arrow, so that the one wounded says: I am wounded with love. In the same way the Antichrist is an arrow of the evil one, and all sinners are arrows of the devil, which he uses against the righteous. Look at a woman, and they have plotted against you. Is she not a fiery arrow, with fire in her mouth so that she may speak and burn you, fire in her hand, in her whole body, in her whole soul? God sets a bow in the cloud to end the storm, so that there may be no flood. In the opposite way, the evil one uses a bow to end the calm of the soul, to quench peace, to stir up war and to make a storm. But perhaps the poor and needy are the brothers of the upright in heart, the poor in spirit, whom the demons seek to cast down. If you see someone made to stumble and overpowered by sin, understand that this man has been slaughtered and his blood is flowing, and God requires that blood. For his vital power has perished, and God requires it from brother and from beast: from the believer who causes others to stumble, from the one who is a stranger to the faith, and from the hand of the watchman.

(72) But perhaps these things have been treated with too much elaboration. The psalmist, however, makes plain everything already said, namely: The sinner observes the righteous man. As if on a painted panel, he clearly depicts the sinner raging, brings him forward in battle array and shows him murderous, baring his sword and already shooting, and so he makes the sinner's unrighteousness vivid. The sinner's targets are not someone who has wronged him, or offended him in some way, or given him reasonable grounds for war in self-defense. His aim is to cast down the poor man, that is, the gentle, modest and lowly in heart, whom the Savior also called poor in spirit and said is worthy of the kingdom of heaven. What quarrel, then, do sinners have with the upright in heart and the poor in spirit? None whatever. Those men have done them no wrong, but direct their own ways toward righteousness. What sharpens the ones named against them, I think, is simply a vain and groundless envy, kindled in them by diabolical perversity.
Verse 15. May their sword enter into their own hearts, and may their bows be broken.
Just as the peace of the righteous returns to him, so may the sword of the ungodly enter into his own heart, if the upright in heart keeps watch over himself.
Verse 16. Better is a little for the righteous than the great wealth of sinners.

The plain wording has something useful for the simpler readers, but it also has something said in a hidden way for those who know how to hear Scripture more deeply. The simpler sense is this. The righteous and the unrighteous both earn a living. The righteous seek what they need only so far as righteousness allows: either they gain nothing, or they gain without injustice and color what they gain with righteousness. The unrighteous are wholly bent on gain, so as to acquire much, and they do not ask whether they acquire it honestly. Two things, then, are set before us, a small gain with righteousness and a large one with injustice, and Better is a little for the righteous than the great wealth of sinners. Let us also look at the hidden sense. It is better to be an unlearned believer who cannot even open his mouth than to be rich in spoken eloquence and in learning while living in wickedness or unbelief.
Verse 17. For the arms of sinners will be broken, but the Lord upholds the righteous.

Suppose you see the vigor and strength of the ungodly man broken, so that he cannot stretch out his hand to a good deed, because it is broken. Then you will see that this has been fulfilled: The arms of sinners will be broken. The one who breaks them is the devil. Every man, however, is weak, and left to himself he falls down. He needs the one who upholds those who fall and raises up those who have been dashed to the ground.
Verse 21. The sinner borrows and will not repay, but the righteous has compassion and gives.

In a loftier sense: when Paul, or some other of the sacred guides into the mysteries, teaches, the hearers borrow tested silver from Paul's mouth. The righteous man pays back the interest and says: You gave me a mina; see, I have made ten minas. You gave me five talents; see, I have ten. But the sinner spends everything. One is not permitted to lend one's own money, that is, to teach as the heretics do. One must lend God's tested silver, like the one who says: Or do you seek proof of the Christ who speaks in me? The principal must be repaid with interest through conduct and action. Otherwise it is better not to borrow at all, especially from the Lord's treasury, than to lose the king's money.
Verse 22. For those who bless him will inherit the earth, but those who curse him will be utterly destroyed.

(73) This is like what was said to Abraham: I will bless those who bless you, and I will curse those who curse you. So if God is the one who has compassion and gives, those who glorify him for this, that is, who bless him, will be heirs of the land promised to the saints. They will receive the good and spacious land, which is not a mere center or point. (74) If we lay a curse on the righteous man, we are in danger of final destruction. For the Lord says to the righteous: I will be an enemy to your enemies and will oppose those who oppose you. And just as he says, 'You fed this one, you fed me,' it follows that one may say, 'You reviled this one, you reviled me.' Those who do not know God curse him, sometimes even hurling [?] words against his glory, to the point that they cannot bear to give him thanks even for the benefits they have received (75). The nations bless Christ, and therefore they inherit the kingdom; but the Jews blaspheme him and are utterly destroyed.
Verse 23. A man's steps are directed by the Lord, and he will greatly desire his way.

(76) As with his own child, he says, God takes him by the hand and leads him onto a straight road. He does not let him run crookedly or make the tracks of his life winding, but leads him straight toward every good thing, teaching and directing them, as in the verse: You held my right hand and guided me by your counsel. When a man's steps have been directed by the Lord, then he will desire his way. (77) The phrase is ambiguous. It may mean that the Lord desires the way of the one whose steps are directed and accepts the course he takes according to the law, while not desiring the way of the ungodly or of those who walk crookedly. Or it may mean that the man whose steps are directed by the Lord desires the way of the Lord, because in having his steps directed he has tasted the sweetness of the way in which the Lord directed him. But it is perhaps better to understand that the Lord will desire the man's way, that is, will make it desirable and accept it. Just as he holds the ways of the lawless as undesired, so he makes desirable the ways of those who do good. And what pleases God is altogether excellent and full of every praise, for God would not have desired what is not so. Those who belong to the heresies do walk in steps, but not steps directed by the Lord. Their steps have been made crooked by the evil one. They turn aside to right and left, not content with simple faith, and understand things more deeply, but not truly. The Lord does not desire their way, because their steps are not those of men but of a wild beast, a reptile or cattle.
Verse 24. When he falls he will not be dashed down, for the Lord supports his hand.

Wrestlers in the contests have fallen in the first bout and won the three falls. Of them you might say, in a bodily sense: He has fallen, but he has not been dashed down, for he has won after falling. Suppose you see a man who has been defeated, yet after his defeat he has not given himself over to licentiousness to practice every kind of impurity. Instead he has risen up, remembering the Scripture: Does the one who falls not rise up? Or does the one who turns away not turn back? Then say that such a man, though he fell, has not been dashed down. But if after falling he gives up, he has been dashed down. It is good, then, to be an athlete who never falls, or, to use terms taken from the examples, one who is never caught round the waist and never pinned. But if he has fallen, let him rise. For the fallen are mourned, and so are those who after sinning have grown callous and given themselves over to every sin. Among the beardless youths (78) [?], be crowned among the men. Have you fallen among the boys? Compete among the beardless youths and win there. In the womb Jacob took Esau by the heel; from boyhood Daniel prophesied and refuted the elders. Can you not become such a person? Then become an athlete afterwards, like the righteous man, who, even if he falls while wrestling or running, is not dashed down, because the Lord supports his hand. The phrase is ambiguous: it may mean the Lord's own hand, or the hand of the wrestler who is already about to be dashed down, so that he does not go down entirely on his face and end up lying flat on the ground.
Verse 25. I was young, and indeed I have grown old, and I have not seen the righteous forsaken.

We also know, in another way, the ages of the inner man: child, youth and old man. Before Abraham, at any rate, those who lived longer than he did are not called elders. He was the first to be called an elder, because of his virtue and because his inner man had put away childish things. And listen to Jeremiah: Do not say, 'I am too young.' Understand something like this about David as well: I was an infant, he says, according to my inner man. But I changed from a youthful and unstable character, in which I behaved like a youth and so was younger, and I came to old age, with a spotless life and gray-haired wisdom. Having advanced in this way, I have not seen the righteous forsaken. If you take this in a bodily sense, it is false. There are two kinds of being forsaken. One is bodily, and it does us no harm. The other is of the soul, and it is deadly. The richer we are in righteous works, the more we are helped not to be forsaken to the end. That is why he did not say 'one who was forsaken' but 'one left forsaken.' For the righteous are indeed forsaken for a time, like Job, so that they may be shown to be righteous.
PSALM 41
Verse 10. I will say to God: You are my helper; why have you forgotten me? And why do I go about downcast while the enemy oppresses me?
Verse 11. While my bones were being crushed, my enemies reproached me, saying to me every day: Where is your God?

Not all of us see how God shows mercy. Often what happens by his mercy is painful, and because it displeases us we do not even consider it mercy. That is why we say: Why have you forgotten me? But anyone who has grasped that everything God brings upon us he brings for our benefit will say nothing of the kind. He knows that God does this in working for his repentance and his good. But, as we were saying, the repentant people asks God why he has forsaken it, so oppressed and downcast. (80) What is the cause of such abandonment? It seems to be no ordinary one. The one who says, Why have you forgotten me?, seems confident, as though he has done nothing for which God would forget him. And the righteous man is greatly grieved when 'Where?' is said of God, since the word signifies place. For it is the height of folly to think that God is in a place. Place goes together with bulk, but the Divine is free of bulk. These words of the prayer also suit the people in Babylon. He means: I always enjoyed your providence, and now I have been stripped bare. I lament because I cannot bear the enemies who, amid blows and chains and the crushing of my bones, say, Where is your God?, supposing that I suffer these things because of his weakness. In a more moral sense: when our enemies the demons crush our bones through sin, that is, the powers of the soul, then they deliberately slander God to us as weak. They do this so that they may draw us away from our hope in him and take us as captives and slaves. And they do it every day, that is, continually. What, then, must we do? We must not fall into despair, but hope in the mercy of God, as we are taught in what follows.
PSALM 50
Verse 7. For behold, I was conceived in iniquities.
Not only in the womb, but also because the works of lawlessness took hold of me: the works of murder, and of another man's bed, which I plundered in violation of the law.
Verse 8. For behold, you have loved truth.

The sense is this: "You, Lord," he says, "being true and loving truth, and wishing us to live in truth, will purge us of the ancient sin; and you will purge us so thoroughly that we are made whiter than snow." This purging will come to us through hyssop, and the working of the Holy Spirit is likened to hyssop, since it warms us and scours away all the filth within us. "For behold, when I had renounced Satan…" — "You have loved." The Wisdom of the Father is plainly the Word, and the hidden and secret things of the Word are the doctrine of the incarnation. "Yet I neglected all these things, and I slipped and fell." "In this way," he says, "you will judge. Some you will punish and others you will crown, since you cherish the truth. And since you cherish the truth and know the weakness of our nature, grant pardon to those who ask for the remedies." Because one who has been trained in sophistry and then turns to the contemplation of truth, once he has learned its greatness, comes to love it perfectly. For those who have not been trained in falsehoods become more clear-sighted and perceive the admirable beauty of truth. Such were Moses and Daniel: after they had experienced sophistical arguments, they rose to true wisdom itself and received testimony from God that they were perfectly wise, for God revealed to them the hidden and secret things of his wisdom, so that nothing was obscure or shadowy to them. David too [?] that he has attained this state, in the present verse: "For you have not only set me on the seats of worldly power, but also counted me worthy of the grace of prophecy. You have revealed beforehand what will soon come to pass, and made plain to me things that are unspeakable to others: the incarnation of your Only-begotten, and the salvation of the world that comes from it."
Psalm 77
Verse 30. While the food was still in their mouths,
Verse 31. the wrath of God rose up against them, and slew many of them, and hobbled the chosen of Israel.

When the Hebrews saw the quail, they did not believe the promise of God, who had undertaken to feed them to the full for a month. Fearing that the quail might fly away or be used up again, "they spread them out," it says, "to dry around the camp. And the meat was still between their teeth, before it was gone, and the Lord was angry with the people, and the Lord struck the people with a very great plague." The great plague was the death of many, as is said here: "He slew among the greater number," that is, many. Oh, what ingratitude! Before the meat between their teeth was used up, they lost faith and forgot the power of God. So they were indeed filled with what they craved, as a demonstration of God's providence toward them; but because of their unbelief and greed it turned into the disease of cholera for them, and many perished of it. Their example was enough to teach self-restraint both to those people themselves and to all who look back on them.

For "among the greater number," Aquila and Symmachus rendered "among the fat and sleek," by which they meant the richer and stronger of the people, since it is likely that these gorged themselves more greedily for that very reason. According to the Seventy, however, he slew "among the greater number," that is, many, and David also called them "chosen," as being warriors. These numbered six hundred thousand five hundred and fifty, from twenty years old and upward, not counting those younger, the women, and the whole tribe of Levi. All these God fed to satiety for a long time. For he said: "You shall eat for a whole month, until it comes out of your nostrils." He saw a people full of craving and wished to cleanse them of it, and he saw that they would not be cleansed by a word of teaching, but would be sated by the very craving once it was fulfilled. For there is satiety in all things, not only in sleep but also in food. Therefore he sent them quail for thirty days; and they, giving in to their greed, perished of a choleric disorder.

I find that the people ate quail twice: once immediately after they came out of the land of Egypt, and the second time, as recorded in Numbers, when they spoke ill of the bread of God and called it worthless. It was then that wrath rose up against them, as though it had been somewhere below before they sinned. For though they had had much experience of God's power, they did not believe that the Lover of mankind could supply them with food. So he both gave them the food and brought the chastisement, showing that he is able to do both: to provide good things and to inflict punishments. We must therefore flee from delicacy-eating, voracity, and gluttony; that is, from immoderation in the use of fine foods, from madness of the throat, from intemperance in eating, and from madness of the belly, so that we may not bury the mind in [?].

There is no harm, however, in considering these stories by way of anagogy as well. God is always rescuing us too from the land of Egypt, from the iron furnace of sin, in order to bring us, through many trials and many wonders, through bread from heaven and through water from the rock (and the rock is Christ), into the holy promise. It would be a great thing for me, then, if, having understood the sea of life, the waves within life, and the bitter, salty surge of worldly affairs, I were enabled by God's kindness to see the spiritual Egyptians and the spiritual Pharaoh drowned; while I myself, in the light of day, might be sheltered by the light cloud, and by the illumination of fire whenever things are dark and difficult. The world is darkened and everything is filled with ignorance, but I, against the spiritual [hosts] of wickedness [?], may be in the light because of the true light, Christ, and because of the cloud. Its formation [?] did not come from vapors in the ordinary course of nature, as when the air is thickened with vapors into a misty mass and compressed upon itself by the winds; it was something better and higher than human comprehension. Even when the sun's rays shone hotly, it served as a barrier, shading what lay beneath and moistening the fiery air with a fine dew; and by night it became fire from evening until morning, lighting a great radiance for the Israelites with its own light. And it would be a great thing if, in the wilderness of life, where great folly in affairs prevails, he would split open his most solid word, which is called a rock, and give me drink without stint and to the full, so that the flowing water might be compared to an abyss, and to the rivers that flow from the spiritual belly.

But I provoke the Most High in the waterless place if, after receiving the teaching, I sin again, forgetting the words that nourished me and the water from the rock, which is Christ. Christ is likened to a rock because he cannot be broken or shaken, for the divine and supreme nature stands firm in its own goodness. The synagogue spoke against him too, as they once did against Moses, accusing him before Pilate and crying out, "Away with him, crucify him!" Then they grieved him with two blows, just as Moses struck the rock twice: they killed the Author of life, and then they tried to persuade people that he had remained among the dead. But the rock poured forth its stream abundantly and gave drink to the whole congregation, for Christ flooded the world with holy and divine streams. He who makes the divine stream gush for the thirsty, and pours out water from his side when the iron opened that vein, also turned the bitterness of Marah, that is, of the punishing law, into sweetness, through the acceptance of the wood of the cross and of the mystery accomplished on it. For the letter and the law kill, but the Spirit and the gospel's worship in the Spirit give life.

God takes great care for man: he opens heaven to him and gives him heavenly food, and he himself leads him by the hand, becoming a light for those on the journey and guiding them on paths that human nature does not know by itself. But he sends down the quail in the evening and the manna at dawn, and by this example he hints to us indirectly that the lover of earthly things is not in the spiritual light. Earthly things are signified by the quail, which God holds out to those who seek it; he does not himself draw them into desire, but neither does he yet grant them mastery over the passions [?]. The manna, on the other hand, is a shadow of the teachings and gifts that come through Christ, which are from above and from heaven, have nothing earthy about them, and have still less to do with fleshly foulness. So the right and unadulterated knowledge of these things is the food of spirits, and it is supplied as in light and daytime, when the Sun of righteousness, the Lord, rises and nourishes us to unending life.

For whoever has eaten the divine manna will rise above corruption and leap beyond death. "Each shall gather," it says, "with those of his tent, and you shall leave none of it until morning." For together with those who share our faith, who dwell in the tent, the Church, we must take our fill of our divine words, and not hold on to the shadow after the truth has been revealed. "For you who would be justified by the law," it says, "have fallen from grace." Yet now that we have come through faith to the sabbath rest understood in Christ, that is, to rest and cessation from sin, we do not reject as useless the instruction of the law that was laid up beforehand, which leads us by the hand to Christ. For we turn to the shadows given through Moses in order to seek the truth within them, bringing out of the treasure things new and old. Or, if you prefer: what we gather here on the day of preparation, we shall find there when we keep the sabbath, and we shall be nourished by it.

Of old, then, God gave his people bread from heaven, which without any toil could satisfy every taste, for it changed into whatever anyone wished. Such is the nature of the word that nourishes the soul: it changes according to the capacity of the one being nourished. If the law nourishes an infant, it becomes milk; if a sick soul, vegetables; if one who is mature, solid food. The manna does not come to us while we sit still, but when we go out of the camp, by which I mean the body in which the soul is confined. For the soul must no longer be in the flesh, but in the spirit. No one who bears the image of the earthy can eat heavenly bread, for the natural man [?] … name to the bread [?]. Pray that God may send us provisions to the full, not only so that we may taste, but so that we may be filled with the words of life and strengthened by them. This, however, is the primary food.

Once, while they were eating the manna, the Hebrews said: "There is nothing at all before our eyes but this manna. For we remember how we sat by the pots of meat in Egypt." We pity them as people who sinned back then, without seeing that the same sins happen among us. Instead of the spiritual Scripture we long to eat the foul-smelling leeks, the onions that harm the eyes of the soul, and the garlic, that is, the sins that fill us with stench, and to gorge ourselves on the rank odors of pleasure. Longing for the slackness of the world and of bodily things, we crave melons; and choosing what does not pass into the substance of the soul, we want to eat cucumbers. And since we do not want the bread from heaven, whose heralds are the prophets and the righteous, who are called clouds because their minds are borne on high and because, like clouds [?], they water us with spiritual rains, God will send us something else: meat like dust, until it comes out of our nostrils and fills us with disease and sickness, since we seek after sin, which reeks and brings many tears.

Those who enjoy worldly things are sick in soul; that is why they suffer cholera and disease and every evil, because of their double-mindedness. But may we fast an acceptable fast, not feeding the mind of the flesh. May we not be found in a waterless place, deprived of the spiritual waters, through doing nothing that sweetens the kindness of the Most High; and it is sweetened by what is done and contemplated in virtue and wisdom. Nor may we tempt him in our hearts, that is, doubt the power of God, not superficially but from the depths of our governing faculty. Nor may we ask for food for our souls; I do not mean the souls made in God's image, which are nourished by the bread of life, but the souls that turn into flesh because they have grown attached to material things, and which crave not wholesome and beneficial food but food that is pleasant and causes disease. Instead, may a table be prepared for us, on which Wisdom sets out her sacrifices and mixes her wine in the bowl. Nor may wrath rise up against us, the deceitful spirit of the ruler [of this world], which, like a forerunner or a spy, rises up into the soul from the darkness where it had lain hidden, by way of our thoughts; nor may it be kindled like fire by the flaming arrows of the enemy. Rather, may the windows of heaven be opened to us, those of spiritual and intelligible [?] … virtues; vices [are the gates] of Hades and death [?], which, according to Peter, do not prevail over those who have gone up to the gates of the daughter of Zion. And may the man hidden in the heart, made in the image of God, become a companion of the angels, partaking of the true manna and food from heaven, not from the accursed earth, which the sinner eats in sorrow. Let those who hear these things take wing and be lifted up; let them no longer be in the flesh, but in the spirit. For those who are in the flesh cannot please God. But we must return to the history.
Verse 44. And he turned their rivers into blood, and their rainwater, so that they could not drink.

I know that, in the figurative sense, there are many rivers of Egypt opposed to Christ, the true river, whose streams gladden the Church. These are all the currents foreign to salvation, which God turns into blood whenever he wishes to convert some people, so that they may come out and drink from the rock; and the rock was Christ. For when I [?] of foreign water and foreign thinking, once God has shown [?] that it is blood, I no longer drink it, so that I may not share in that bloody rainwater. These would be the people whose words are few but deadly. As for the history, the Egyptians have no water from above, and no rain falls in Egypt. Historically, then, when all the water throughout Egypt was turned into blood at that time by Moses' command, so that even the fish perished because the water had been changed into a fleshy thickness, there was no blood for the Hebrews when they drew water. That is how the sorcery found its opportunity to counterfeit the bloody water, using the water found among the Hebrews. Spiritually, the same thing can be seen happening even now. Among those who are divided by opposing beliefs, for some the stream of faith that they draw through divine teaching is drinkable and clear, while for those who play the Egyptian in their evil opinions the water becomes corrupted blood. And the sophistry of deception often tries to turn even the Israelites' drink, that is, our doctrine, into blood by the defilement of falsehood, and to show it to us as something other than what it is. Yet it cannot make the drink wholly useless, even if by deceit it reddens its surface appearance. For the Israelite drinks the true water and pays no attention to the deceptive appearance.
Psalm 80
Verse 2. Shout aloud to the God of Jacob.

They call the Savior the God of Jacob, since he appeared to Jacob in human form as a sign of the incarnation that would come later. They bid us shout aloud, sending up a hymn of victory to him for destroying the one who held the power of death and for rescuing us from the tyranny of the demons. For a shout of this kind is a victory hymn, which those rescued from Babylon also urge one another to sing to God who gave them the victory. On a more moral level: let those who do what is right, whose fruits come to the winepresses, listen to the words "Rejoice in God." But let the one who has sinned and needs repentance and conversion not rejoice, but be grieved in a godly way. For godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation and brings no regret. And you, if with God's help you have brought in the harvest of your fruits to the holy winepresses, do not forget God, since he is your helper. Even if you lack words worthy of offering to God in thanksgiving, shout aloud with a clear voice, from a heart that cries out beyond anything that halting speech can signify, and that, for lack of words, speaks what is unspeakable and inexpressible. For if you rise above what can be spoken, if you pass beyond what is put into words and voiced by the mouth, and are able to hymn God with the mind alone, the mind being at a loss to put its own movements into speech because the word within you cannot bear the unspeakable and divine things of the mind, then you will shout aloud to the God of Jacob, as an imitator of Jacob the supplanter.
Psalm 150
Verse 3. Praise him with the sound of the trumpet.

Another version says "with the sound of the horn." This is a priestly instrument, for the priests used trumpets to recall the trumpets that sounded at Sinai. So, following the spiritual sense of the instructions for making trumpets, we must make a trumpet so that we may praise God with its sound. Such trumpets, I think, are also meant in the words "The trumpet will sound, and the dead will be raised." And there is a feast, the New Moon of the seventh month, a memorial of trumpets, as it is said: "Blow the trumpet at the new moon."
